paragraphs.narration: New Zealand released stoats to save its farms, and they helped empty its forests instead. By the late 1800s, rabbits were overrunning the country, eating through the sheep pasture that New Zealand's farms depended on. Controlling them became the goal.

The answer seemed obvious: bring in a predator that already hunted rabbits. Stoats, along with ferrets and weasels, were introduced as early as 1879, and stoats were imported and released in 1884, specifically to control the rabbits. People expected the predators to stay on the problem they were brought for.
The stoats did not stay where the rabbits were.

Instead, they spread quickly into forests and areas with no rabbits at all. There, the mechanism that made them useful on farmland turned against the native wildlife. They fed on New Zealand's poorly flighted birds and on their eggs, prey that had evolved with no defense against a fast, climbing mammal.

The clearest picture comes from the kiwi. In a central Northland study of brown kiwi, researchers tracked chick deaths and found stoats were the single largest identified cause. Where the agent could be identified, stoats killed 19 of 31 chicks, about 63 percent. Young kiwi are vulnerable until they reach roughly a kilogram at six to eight months, which is exactly the window stoats exploit.

This was not a single local misfortune. A meta-analysis found that the critical factor in the kiwi's decline on the mainland was predation by introduced mammals, especially stoats killing chicks. The same animals helped exterminate stitchbirds, saddlebacks, kākāpō and little spotted kiwi from the mainland altogether.

The toll still runs today. Only about 5 percent of Northland's brown kiwi chicks reach adulthood, and their biggest threats remain stoats and feral cats. Reversing it is hard: stoats are clever and careful, very suspicious of baits and traps, which makes them difficult to control.

So the predator carried in to protect farmland became the predator most responsible for the forest's losses. Next time a fix means importing one animal to solve a problem, ask which other creatures you are quietly entering into the bargain.

_research_dossier.research_summary: In the 1870s-1880s, New Zealand's European farming economy was being devastated by introduced rabbits, which had been released earlier for food and game. Farmers pressured the government to import mustelids—stoats, ferrets and weasels—as biological control, despite explicit warnings from scientists including ornithologist Walter Buller. Stoats were released from the mid-1880s onward. They failed to control rabbits, instead spreading into forests and preying on New Zealand's flightless and ground-nesting birds, which had evolved without mammalian predators. Stoats are now the primary killer of kiwi chicks: in unmanaged areas roughly 95% of chicks die before reaching breeding age, with stoats the leading identified cause of death. Controlled studies (trapping and 1080) demonstrate the causal link by raising chick survival when stoats are removed. The ledger includes three comparable deliberate/accidental biological-control or invasive-predator failures (Australian cane toads, Guam brown tree snakes, and general invasive-predator extinction statistics) to support the film's closing generalisation. Redundancy is built in so the 10 core factual events each rest on more than one source, budgeting for retrieval attrition from paywalls and quote mismatches.
